newsitem.title: JAPAN: Gore trip to China comes under sudden strain.
newsitem.headline: Gore trip to China comes under sudden strain.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore headed to Beijing on Monday on a trip suddenly strained by a row about possible Chinese efforts to influence U.S. elections.
The controversy cast a cloud over hopes the four-day visit would start to heal ties damaged by recent disputes ranging from human rights to trade and Taiwan.

In comments to reporters shortly before his departure for Beijing after a 24-hour stop in Tokyo, Gore indicated he did not intend to shy away from any subject in his talks with the Chinese leadership.
"I will of course discuss human rights in my meetings with the leadership of China, nor will it be a surprise to them to hear these matters raised," Gore said.

In a sign of its own worries that the political funding issue could get in the way of better relations, China sternly denied charges that it had sought to influence U.S. policy through political contributions.

A signed commentary in the official People's Daily on Monday said Beijing had not made contributions to the U.S. Democratic Party to influence American policy and Gore's visit had no link to improper payments.
"The Chinese government is not involved in the so-called 'political contributions scandal' in the slightest way and is entirely free of guilt," the newspaper said.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year that they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign contributions from foreign corporations.
When he set off on the trip, Gore told reporters he intended to raise the issue in Beijing "in an appropriate way and in the proper context" but stressed that "this is not what this trip is about".

However, during his stopover in Tokyo, the funding issue mushroomed to a point where it is likely to be the first item on the agenda, needing to be put to rest before U.S. and Chinese officials can get down to their real work.
Gore will be the most senior U.S. official to visit China in eight years and hopes to pave the way for an exchange of visits by U.S. President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
"The continuation of high-level visits, such as the visit of U.S. Vice President Gore and others, is due to the efforts of the two governments and their peoples," the Peoples Daily said.

"To insist that this is linked to the so-called contributions scandal is ridiculous," it said. "It is a complete fabrication to allege the improvement in Sino-U.S. relations is due to any improper payments by the Chinese government."
Gore has said he believes his visit at this time has value because "both our countries are clearly signalling to one another that we want to find a way to move forward in the relationship".
Although U.S. officials were negotiating with their Chinese counterparts to try to hammer out various agreements in time for Gore's trip, no dramatic breakthroughs are expected.

In fact, Gore's advisers had a debate over whether he should even participate in a signing ceremony in which China plans to order new jet airplanes from Boeing Co, a move that will generate jobs and benefit the U.S. economy.

Although officials said there was no doubt Gore would participate in such an event if a final contract was reached, the fact there was any question underscored the sensitivity of the political funding issue.
